 9                THE SECRETARY:   Resolution Number 

10   3338, by Senators Stewart-Cousins and Larkin, 

11   commemorating the observance of the 31st Annual 

12   Martin Luther King, Jr. Day in the State of 

13   New York, on January 18, 2016.  

14                "WHEREAS, From time to time we take 

15   note of certain individuals whom we wish to 

16   recognize for their valued contributions and to 

17   publicly acknowledge their endeavors which have 

18   enhanced the basic humanity among us all; and 

19                "WHEREAS, Attendant to such concern,  

20   and in full accord with its long-standing 

21   traditions, it is the custom of this Legislative 

22   Body to join the people of this great Empire 

23   State in proudly observing the 31st Annual Martin 

24   Luther King, Jr. Day in the State of New York, on 

25   January 18, 2016, taking note of his many 


                                                                214

 1   accomplishments and contributions to mankind; and 

 2                "WHEREAS, Dr. Martin Luther King, 

 3   Jr., was born the grandson of a slave into a 

 4   segregated society in Atlanta, Georgia, on 

 5   January 15, 1929, and was instrumental in  

 6   formulating a policy which ultimately destroyed 

 7   legal apartheid in the southern states of our 

 8   nation; and 

 9                "WHEREAS, In February of 1968, 

10   Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., spoke about the 

11   inevitability of his death and hoped that when we 

12   spoke of his life, we would not concentrate on 

13   his academic achievements:  that he graduated  

14   from Morehouse College, that he attended the 

15   Crozer Theological Seminary and Boston 

16   University, where he earned a doctorate in 

17   systematic theology; and 

18                "WHEREAS, Furthermore, Dr. Martin 

19   Luther King, Jr., did not find it important that 

20   we mention that he won the Nobel Peace Prize and 

21   over 300 other awards; and 

22                "WHEREAS, Dr. Martin Luther King,  

23   Jr.'s finest legacy of greater social justice for 

24   all Americans was truly reflected in his devotion  

25   to serve and respect others, and in his steadfast 


                                                                215

 1   love for all humanity; and 

 2                "WHEREAS, Standing in a long line of 

 3   great American black leaders, Dr. Martin Luther 

 4   King, Jr., represents the historical culmination 

 5   and the living embodiment of a spirit of united 

 6   purpose rooted in black African culture and the 

 7   American dream; and 

 8                "WHEREAS, An apostle of peace, 

 9   Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., fought unrelentingly 

10   for the civil rights of all Americans and taught  

11   us that through nonviolence, courage displaces 

12   fear, love transforms hate, acceptance dissipates 

13   prejudice, and mutual regard cancels enmity; and 

14                "WHEREAS, Dr. Martin Luther King, 

15   Jr., manifestly contributed to the cause of 

16   America's freedom, and his commitment to human 

17   dignity is visibly mirrored in the spiritual, 

18   economic and political dimensions of the civil 

19   rights movement; and 

20                "WHEREAS, In addition, Dr. Martin 

21   Luther King, Jr.'s life was devoted to the 

22   liberation of his people, and his courage  

23   transcended the advocates of mindless 

24   retrenchment; and 

25                "WHEREAS, It is the sense of this 


                                                                216

 1   Legislative Body that the common and shared  

 2   responsibility of governance demands an  

 3   irrevocable commitment to the preservation and  

 4   enhancement of human dignity as exemplified by 

 5   Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.; and 

 6                "WHEREAS, Upon the occasion of the 

 7   celebration of the birthday of Dr. Martin Luther 

 8   King, Jr., it is the practice of this Legislative 

 9   Body to commemorate the heroic efforts of 

10   Dr. King, who loved and served humanity, and who 

11   was a drum major for peace, justice and 

12   righteousness; and 

13                "WHEREAS, The 2016 Dr. Martin Luther  

14   King, Jr., holiday observance marks the 

15   87th anniversary of his birth, and the 31st 

16   annual holiday celebrated in the State of 

17   New York in his honor; now, therefore, be it 

18                "RESOLVED, That this Legislative 

19   Body pause in its deliberations to memorialize 

20   and pay tribute to the legendary life and 

21   achievements of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., upon 

22   the occasion of the anniversary of his birth and 

23   the celebration of Martin Luther King, Jr., Day 

24   in the State of New York and throughout the 

25   nation; and be it further 


                                                                217

 1                "RESOLVED, That a copy of this  

 2   resolution, suitably engrossed, be transmitted to  

 3   the Black, Puerto Rican, Hispanic and Asian 

 4   Legislative Caucus."

 5                ACTING PRESIDENT GRIFFO:   Senator 

 6   Stewart-Cousins.

 7                SENATOR STEWART-COUSINS:   Thank 

 8   you, Mr. President.

 9                I rise, as we do annually, to give 

10   honor to a man who has not only changed the 

11   course of everyday lives of individuals, but our 

12   understanding of peace and equality and service 

13   and justice in our world.

14                I often talk about my parents, who 

15   had no thought of me ever being in a position 

16   such as this because of the world they lived in 

17   as African-Americans.  

18                But the reality is that we are at 

19   this point where Dr. King's message has to be 

20   more resonant within each of us in the work that 

21   we do today than ever before.  There's a lot of 

22   opinions, there's a lot of conversation.  And we 

23   in this chamber have the ability to lead in ways 

24   that would make Dr. King proud.  

25                One of his quotes that I remember is 


                                                                218

 1   "life's persistent question is what can you do 

 2   for others."  We are all in the position every 

 3   day to do something for others.  But few of us 

 4   are in these kinds of positions that when we act, 

 5   we are doing for others.  

 6                What will we do?  What will we do in 

 7   reforming criminal justice?  What will we do in 

 8   education?  What will we do in economic justice?  

 9   What will we do to make sure that equality is the 

10   key to America's continued progress right here in 

11   this state?

12                That's the persistent question.  And 

13   fortunately for us in this chamber, we can offer 

14   the answer.  I hope that next year when we 

15   celebrate Dr. King's birthday, we will have spent 

16   our days leading up to it answering, in the way 

17   Dr. King would have us answer, life's persistent 

18   question.

19                Thank you.

23   Mr. President.

24                Thank you, Senator Cousins.

25                I had never met Dr. King until March 


                                                                219

 1   of 1965.  In August of '63, I was in Europe, and 

 2   we were aware of all of the marching going on in 

 3   Washington and what some of our brightest people 

 4   said "This will turn into something bigger."  And 

 5   it did.

 6                March the 7th, the United States of 

 7   America should be ashamed of that day, because 

 8   that's the day we had people with baseball bats, 

 9   with guns and everything else, shooting at people 

10   because they were of color.  Or they were people 

11   of noncolor supporting people of color.  That 

12   slaughter on that day was an opening eye to a lot 

13   of people.  

14                About 5 o'clock that night my phone 

15   rang, and thinking about who would be calling me 

16   at 5 o'clock on Sunday night, and it was the 

17   sergeant major.  And he said, "There will be a 

18   car in front of your house in 15 minutes.  Plan 

19   to be here all night."  So I packed up and went 

20   to the Pentagon.

21                And right then and there, the 

22   President had already given instructions, 

23   something has to be done.  The chief of staff of 

24   the Army, John Sullivan, said, "You fight fire 

25   with fire.  But this is more than fire, this is 


                                                                220

 1   human dignity."

 2                I was never so ashamed of people.  I 

 3   saw that film that today we would have seen it 

 4   different ways, we would have known better about 

 5   it.  But this was a total disgrace.  And the real 

 6   meaning of it was that the American people didn't 

 7   rise up and say:  What the hell is going on in 

 8   our country?  This is a disgrace.  We're 

 9   Americans.  Do we beat one another to death?

10                Well, I was very emotional and said 

11   my piece:  The only way we're going to do this is 

12   we must control it.  The President then said, 

13   "Number one, let's ask Governor Wallace to 

14   activate his troops."  That wasn't going to be 

15   the school solution in my opinion.  But as a 

16   young major waiting to make -- three weeks later 

17   to become a colonel, I was very careful what I 

18   said, Michael.  You eat some of those words.

19                The orders first came out to hand 

20   this message to Wallace.  And I did, on the 10th.  

21   And he told me to tell the President where to 

22   shove that paper.  I came back to Montgomery Air 

23   Base, called Washington.  They said:  "Stay there 

24   till midnight and open the second package."  So I 

25   opened the second package and went back.  


                                                                221

 1                And this colonel down there -- by 

 2   now I have changed from civilian clothes to "I'm 

 3   also a major," and I said:  "Here is an another 

 4   order for your governor.  And tell him that 

 5   somebody has to sign this tonight."  Somebody 

 6   come out and signed it.  It ordered all of 

 7   Alabama military -- National Guard, reserves, 

 8   air, whatever it was -- were being called to 

 9   active duty by the President.  

10                And there are some people who still 

11   say to you, Well, Wallace did this because if he 

12   activated Alabama troops, Alabama citizens would 

13   have paid for the mission.  But when the 

14   President paid for them, all of us that were 

15   alive in those days, we paid for it.

16                I didn't care.  He got the message.  

17   And he told me where to go.  I didn't go there.   

18   I went back to Washington.  

19                We went back later.  The idea was, 

20   in my opinion Wallace was the key because nobody 

21   did what they did without the governor's 

22   blessing.  But there was a police chief, his name 

23   was Bull Connor.  I don't know if any of you ever 

24   heard of him.  Overweight, obese -- Kemp Hannon 

25   would be telling him what to do to reduce his 


                                                                222

 1   calories.  

 2                I went to see him because I thought 

 3   he was the bull in the china closet.  And he said 

 4   to me, "I don't talk to tin soldiers."  My answer 

 5   to him was very simple.  "If you stand on that 

 6   bridge on Sunday, your ass" -- excuse me, ladies 

 7   and gentlemen -- "will be thrown in jail for a 

 8   hell of a long time, because you're a brutal, 

 9   dumb-assed member of law enforcement who should 

10   be ashamed of yourself to allow that to happen."

11                The next issue was what do we do.  

12   So we had to come up -- those of you who have 

13   been with the armed forces know we come up with a 

14   compact.  How did we do it?  We brought forces in 

15   from many, many states, all combat units.  And 

16   the one thing we did, we did not put anybody from 

17   Alabama in charge of any of the marching, the 

18   crossings, the collective information, because we 

19   wanted an issue.

20                The President said:  "I want it as 

21   smooth as can be and I don't want any more 

22   disturbance."  I'm proud to stand here to say 

23   today that we marched from the 21st to the 25th, 

24   when we ended up in Montgomery at the state 

25   house.


                                                                223

 1                One thing that bothered me with all 

 2   of this is there was a gentleman there today -- 

 3   where's Bill?  Where's Perkins?  No, that's all 

 4   right, John, don't go get him.

 5                Bill Perkins has a constituent of 

 6   his who was my bodyguard in Alabama.  And 

 7   Montgomery and I have struck up a business of 

 8   friendship, every year we communicate at 

 9   Christmas.  And I don't know, but we're doing 

10   Easter cards this year, right?  I don't know what 

11   happened.  

12                But what did we really accomplish?  

13   There was nobody injured, nobody hurt until the 

14   very last day.  Everybody that marched down this 

15   road we said, Fine, but don't go back that road, 

16   come back this road.  And a lady from 

17   International Auto Workers out of Detroit, 

18   Michigan, her name was Viola Liuzzo, was shot and 

19   killed.  She went into a gin mill, and they were 

20   celebrating.  

21                The celebration that they had should 

22   have been a very nice celebration, in honor, 

23   marching with Dr. King, people of all faiths, 

24   people of all colors, with one mission.  

25                A congressman from California named 


                                                                224

 1   Murphy said at the last day, "Major, if you were 

 2   a member of Congress and you were going to vote 

 3   on this Voting Act, how would you vote?"  I said:  

 4   "Very simple.  They are United States of America 

 5   citizens, and I would let them vote."  We won't 

 6   let them go to my bathroom, they won't let me 

 7   drink out of your water fountain, but I can send 

 8   you, the government of the United States, into 

 9   combat and have some of our youngest men, women, 

10   killed.  It's not a gift we're going to give you.  

11   It's a right we're going to grant you to use and 

12   exercise as you see fit.

13                One of the things that bothered me 

14   yet -- I mentioned it last year.  And Andrea, I 

15   thank you very much for offering to come down to 

16   my armory and see what we did.  We should be 

17   talking about what we are doing.  Dr. King stood 

18   up there and talked.  He gave us a message.  How 

19   many of you walk away from here today and say:  

20   Oh, a couple of politicians stood up there and 

21   shot the bull, for what?

22                For what?  To make the United States 

23   of America a united states, not a divided states.  

24   We cannot live without another one.  Bitching and 

25   moaning about this one does that and this one 


                                                                225

 1   does that -- what have we done about saying we 

 2   must start teaching our young people?  Someone 

 3   says, well, you got to get their grandma and 

 4   grandpa.  

 5                Grandma and grandpa.  I'm grandpa.  

 6   I'm 88 years old next week.  I'm worried about 

 7   those young kids.  If we don't get these kids on 

 8   the right road today, they'll be in the same boat 

 9   and attitude of many of our older people today.  

10   They've lived in a vacuum about it.  And what we 

11   should be doing now is saying, what can we do to 

12   make life honest, real, people looking to talk to 

13   one another?  

14                I invite every one of you to come to 

15   my district.  We call it the Newburgh United.  

16   Saturday of this week that just passed, 68 young 

17   kids -- black, Caucasian, Hispanic and others -- 

18   were playing chess, inner city kids, 68 young 

19   kids played chess.  Somebody said, "I would never 

20   have thought I'd see this."  Why?  Because we 

21   interacted adults with children.  That is what 

22   Dr. King said.  He had a dream about what we 

23   would do and what we can do.  

24                In 1968, he listened to people to 

25   tell him to go to Tennessee, and he was shot.  


                                                                226

 1   What have we done besides a lot of people 

 2   hollering, a lot of hot air, and we're going to 

 3   do this, we're going to do that?  They do what 

 4   they think is best for them.  

 5                That was not what Dr. King was all 

 6   about.  It was about us.  We, the United States 

 7   of America, our young people, our middles, 

 8   seniors.  

 9                Ladies and gentlemen, you want to 

10   see something happen?  Go back in your district 

11   and do it.  Come down to my district and I'll 

12   show you what we did, it cost me a dollar.  I 

13   bought that armory.  I give it away, though.  And 

14   I didn't get a -- Hannon's over there, didn't 

15   give me the dollar, either.  

16                But I'm telling you, when you see 

17   all these kids go together, we have 70 percent of 

18   this armory is academic, 30 percent is jock.  And 

19   when you want to see the girls play soccer, 

20   Andrea, Saturday morning you got to come.  

21                Remember, I'm not standing here to 

22   hear myself.  I remember what was said.  I 

23   remember what the debriefing was.  And General 

24   Sullivan said if we don't abide by what he was 

25   dictating to us, we will repeat.  And we have 


                                                                227

 1   repeated.  We have Missouri, we have Chicago, we 

 2   have Carolinas.  We'd better start waking up and 

 3   think that we are as responsible as those that 

 4   cause the issues.  

 5                Ladies and gentlemen, I thank you.  

 6   But I'm asking you, when we come back next 

 7   year -- with the help of God, Diane -- we'll be 

 8   able to say this is what we did, we put together, 

 9   we had them working.  Whether it's in our high 

10   schools and ROTC, whether it's in scouting or 

11   whatever it might be.  Put up or shut up is what 

12   the proper English is.  

13                Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for 

14   listening.  

15                Thank you, Mr. President.

16                ACTING PRESIDENT GRIFFO:   Thank 

17   you, Senator Larkin.

18                Senator Hassell-Thompson.

19                SENATOR HASSELL-THOMPSON:   Thank 

20   you, Mr. President.

21                I rise to add my voice to that of 

22   the leadership here and thank Senator 

23   Stewart-Cousins for presenting this resolution 

24   this morning.  And you know, I'm always tempted 

25   to call her Andrea, so I stumbled over that part.  


                                                                228

 1   But today she is the leader of the Democratic 

 2   Conference, and so she is entitled to that due.  

 3   And as she very clearly states, that she nor I 

 4   would be given the due if it were not for the 

 5   work of Dr. King.  

 6                I won't be long today, but I always 

 7   have to stand with her and others who acknowledge 

 8   the fact of how far we have come.  We have come 

 9   as a nation and as a world because of Dr. King.  

10   We want to believe that he only brought freedom 

11   to black people, but he also brought freedom to 

12   people whose minds needed to be free.  Free of 

13   the hate, injustices that they had perpetrated 

14   against their fellow human beings.

15                All of us know Dr. King as an 

16   extraordinary orator, certainly as a vociferous 

17   writer, and his understanding of the human 

18   spirit.  But very few people understand that the 

19   thing that I revere most about him was his 

20   transformational leadership.  And he was not just 

21   about how do we find homeless shelters, but how 

22   do we get to the root of homelessness.  It wasn't 

23   about just feeding the hungry, but what is it 

24   that this country needs to do to ensure that 

25   there is no hunger.  As one of the wealthiest 


                                                                229

 1   countries in the world, it is outrageous that in 

 2   our streets every day how hungry our people are.

 3                And so if we want to really aspire 

 4   to be like Dr. King, the four characteristics of 

 5   transformational leadership are individualized 

 6   influence, idealized influence, inspirational 

 7   motivation, intellectual stimulation, and 

 8   individualized consideration.

 9                Now, those are hard things to do.  

10   Because we sit here and we sometimes forget that 

11   the reason that we've been elected to serve gets 

12   distorted, because we think it becomes about us.  

13   But we have to remember every welfare mother who 

14   struggles to feed her children and who is not 

15   trying to scam the system but trying to ensure 

16   that the American dream happens for her children 

17   and for her family.

18                So today, for those of us who speak 

19   and those of us who think about Dr. King, let's 

20   not idealize him, but let us idealize the dreams.  

21   Let us be real about what it is that we have the 

22   power to do in these chambers, and not stand up 

23   on this day and talk about how wonderful he is 

24   and then next week vote against those principles 

25   for which he gave his life.
